question: Should Arjuna fight the battle against his kinsmen, elders and teachers?

sides.position: He should not fight: he sees no good in killing his own people, wants neither victory nor kingship, and would rather live on alms or be killed unresisting.
arguments: Killing kin brings sin, even though they are aggressors, and no happiness can follow (1.36–37).

Destroying a family destroys its eternal family dharmas; adharma prevails, the women are corrupted, varṇa-mixture arises, the ancestors fall for lack of offerings, and the family-destroyers dwell in hell — 'so we have heard' (1.38–44).
To kill venerable gurus like Bhīṣma and Droṇa for blood-smeared enjoyments is worse than living on alms (2.4–5).
He does not know which outcome is better, and no kingdom, even over the gods, would dispel his grief (2.6–8).

sides.position: He should stand up and fight, without grief, as his own dharma, with equanimity and without attachment to the fruit, resigning all actions to Kṛṣṇa.
arguments: His faintness and unmanliness are unworthy (2.2–3).
The wise do not grieve: the embodied self neither slays nor is slain, only bodies end; even on the contrary view death is inevitable (2.11–30, esp. 2.18).
For a kṣatriya nothing is better than a dharmic battle; refusing brings sin and disgrace, fighting brings heaven or the earth (2.31–37).
Fighting with pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat made the same incurs no sin (2.38); action done with the right only to the act, not its fruit, does not bind (2.47–51).
No one can remain without action; allotted action is better than inaction (3.5, 3.8); act for the holding together of the world, as Janaka did and as Kṛṣṇa himself does (3.20–24).
Resign all actions to me and fight (3.30); one's own dharma, even deficient, is better than another's (3.35).

notes: Recorded from Bhagavad Gītā 1–3 only. The text's own close of the debate lies beyond this chunk (Arjuna's words at 18.73). No reconciliation is attempted at extraction.

question: Are the Vedic rites and the heaven, enjoyment and lordship they yield the final goal ('there is nothing else')?

sides.party: those who delight in the statements of the Veda (veda-vāda-ratāḥ), as reported by the Gītā
sides.position: There is nothing else (nānyad astīti): the goal is heaven, enjoyment and lordship, obtained through the many particular rites.
arguments: (Known only through the Gītā's report.) Their speech offers birth as the fruit of works and abounds in particular rites aimed at enjoyment and lordship (2.43).

sides.position: Such speech is 'flowery' and proclaimed by the undiscerning; the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain; one should be free of the three guṇas, and for the knowing brāhmaṇa all the Vedas are of as much use as a well amid a flood.
arguments: For those attached to enjoyment and lordship, carried away by that speech, resolute understanding is not established in samādhi (2.44).
Be free of the three guṇas, of the pairs of opposites, of acquiring and keeping; be possessed of the self (2.45).
Understanding must become indifferent to what is to be heard and has been heard, and stand steady in samādhi though perplexed by śruti (2.52–53).

The same speaker in 3.9–16 enjoins action for the sake of sacrifice and the keeping of the sacrificial wheel; the criticism of 2.42–44 is aimed at those who are desire-souled, intent on heaven, and say 'there is nothing else'.

notes: The Gītā does not name the school it criticises; commentators connect it with those for whom ritual and its heavenly results are the final aim. Verse 2.46 is read in opposite directions (see the teaching's notes). Recorded from chapters 1–3 only; no reconciliation attempted at extraction.

question: If understanding (buddhi) is superior to action, should one abstain from action?

sides.party: Arjuna's question (and the view that renunciation of action brings perfection)
sides.position: If understanding is held superior to action (cf. 2.49), there is no reason to engage in terrible action; Arjuna asks for the one decisive teaching.
arguments: Kṛṣṇa himself ranked action far below the yoga of understanding (2.49; Arjuna's question 3.1).
Kṛṣṇa's speech seems mixed and confusing (3.2).
The view that actionlessness is reached by not undertaking actions and perfection by renunciation is mentioned in order to be denied (3.4).

sides.position: There is a twofold commitment — of knowledge for the sāṃkhyas and of action for the yogins; actionlessness is not reached by not acting; allotted action, done without attachment and for sacrifice, is to be performed.
arguments: Twofold niṣṭhā declared of old (3.3).
No one can remain a moment without action; the guṇas make everyone act (3.5); action is better than inaction and even the body needs it (3.8).
Action done for sacrifice does not bind (3.9).

For one who delights in the self there is nothing to be done (3.17–18); yet act unattached, since by unattached action one reaches the highest, as Janaka and others did, and for the holding together of the world (3.19–20).

notes: How the two niṣṭhās relate (alternatives for different persons, or stages for one person; whether knowledge alone liberates) is itself one of the main points on which the Gītā's commentators divide; see the registry dispute dsp:works-knowledge-grace. Recorded from chapters 1–3 only; no reconciliation attempted at extraction.
